stemBlocks.value: Think first: To square-root x⁴ you halve the index, giving x².

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p093-q13 from workbook page 93.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write each term as a square.
Apply the difference of two squares.
Test each bracket for further factorisation.

contentBlocks.value: 16y is not a perfect square term, so 9x² − 16y is not a difference of two squares; a sum never factorises this way
Result: No further factorisation is possible

strategyBlocks.value: Write both terms as squares, apply the difference of two squares, then test whether either bracket can be factorised again.

whyThisWorks.value: The square root of 81x⁴ is 9x² because squaring doubles an index, so square-rooting halves it. After one application of the rule you must check the new brackets: here neither is a difference of two squares, because 16y is not a square, so the factorisation stops.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing the square root of 81x⁴ as 9x instead of 9x².
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing the square root of 81x⁴ as 9x instead of 9x².

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the square root of 256y² as 16y² rather than 16y.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Giving the square root of 256y² as 16y² rather than 16y.

commonErrors.misconception: Trying to factorise 9x² + 16y, a sum that does not factorise.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Trying to factorise 9x² + 16y, a sum that does not factorise.

examTip.value: Halve the index when square-rooting a power — x⁴ gives x², and x⁶ would give x³.
